warmup.q: Your Quarkus service logs a client as fd00:10:6:0:0:0:0:10. The partner allowlist has fd00:10:6::10, and the string comparison in your filter says they differ. Are they the same address?
options: No: the logged one has eight groups, so it is a longer address
Yes: :: stands for exactly the zero groups the log spells out
Only if both are in the same /64
No: one of them is an IPv4-mapped address
warmup.why: Every IPv6 address is 128 bits, however it's written. :: replaces a run of zero groups, here the four between 6 and 10, so both strings name the same 128 bits. The JVM's getHostAddress() prints the long form, which is why this mismatch is so common. Compare parsed addresses, or format both to RFC 5952 first.

sections.h: An IPv6 address is 128 bits, written in eight groups and then squeezed
sections.html:
Lesson 3 of this track ended with IPv4 running out: 32 bits give 4.3 billion addresses, IANA handed out its last free blocks in 2011, and NAT keeps the internet going by hiding whole buildings behind one address. IPv6 (RFC 8200) fixes the shortage by brute force. Its addresses are 128 bits, about 3.4 × 10^38 of them, enough to give every subnet on earth 2^64 addresses and still not notice. It is not a future technology: Cloudflare saw 29% of requests from dual-stack clients arrive over IPv6 in 2025, and 67% in India.

Writing 128 bits as dotted decimal would take 16 numbers. So IPv6 writes eight groups of 16 bits in hex, separated by colons:

fd00:0010:0006:0000:0000:0000:0000:0020

That is still long, so two shortening rules apply. Leading zeros in a group may go: 0010 is 10 and 0000 is 0. And one run of all-zero groups may be replaced by ::, which means "as many zero groups as it takes to make eight". The address above becomes fd00:10:6::20, which is api in the lab network. :: may appear once only. In 2001:db8::1::2 nobody could tell how many zeros belong on each side.

The rules are optional, and that causes trouble. fd00:10:6::20, fd00:10:6:0::20, FD00:0010:6::0020 and fd00:10:6:0:0:0:0:20 are all the same address. The last one is what the JVM prints: Inet6Address.getHostAddress() drops leading zeros and never uses ::. Any code that compares addresses as text then breaks: an allowlist of partner addresses, a rate limiter keyed by client address, a log search for one customer's requests, a unique key in a database.

RFC 5952 picks one canonical form, and every tool should print it:

  • lower-case hex, and no leading zeros in a group;
  • :: replaces the longest run of two or more zero groups, and the first such run if two are equally long;
  • a single zero group stays 0, never ::.

So 2001:db8:0:0:1:0:0:1 is 2001:db8::1:0:0:1, and 2001:db8:0:1:1:1:1:1 keeps its lone zero. The lab has you write this formatter, and its tests feed it what the JVM really prints.

Prefixes use lesson 3's notation. fd00:10:6::/64 means the first 64 bits name the network, and the last 64 bits, the interface ID, name a card inside it. Nearly every IPv6 subnet is a /64, because the way hosts pick their own addresses (section 3) needs 64 bits for the interface ID. A company or a home gets a bigger block from its provider, often a /48 or a /56, and cuts /64s from it.

try.title: Read your IPv6 addresses
steps: From the labs folder, start the lab network if it isn't running: docker compose -f env/net.yml up -d. Its dual network is dual stack: app has 10.10.6.10 and fd00:10:6::10, and api has 10.10.6.20 and fd00:10:6::20 with a web server on port 8080.
Print app's IPv6 addresses. Before running the Python lines, write the full 8-group form of fd00:10:6::10 and the canonical form of 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0001:0000:0000:0001 yourself.

On a Mac, ifconfig en0 | grep inet6 shows your Wi-Fi card's IPv6 addresses. If your network has IPv6, look for the words secured and temporary after the global ones: the stable random address and the daily one from the section on scopes.

code.title: in labs/
code.html: docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app ip -6 addr show eth0 docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app python3 -c 'import ipaddress as i; a = i.ip_address("fd00:10:6::10"); print(a.exploded); print(a.compressed); print(i.ip_address("2001:0db8:0000:0000:0001:0000:0000:0001"))'

try.expect:
From one run:

11: eth0@if534: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc noqueue state UP group default  link-netnsid 0
    inet6 fd00:10:6::10/64 scope global nodad
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever
    inet6 fe80::10fc:1ff:fe3b:eb52/64 scope link
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever
fd00:0010:0006:0000:0000:0000:0000:0010
fd00:10:6::10
2001:db8::1:0:0:1

Two addresses on one card: the one Docker assigned (scope global, although it is a unique local address; nodad means Docker skipped the duplicate check) and a link-local one the kernel made itself. Your link-local address will differ, because Docker gives the card a new random MAC each time it starts. In the last line two runs of two zero groups tie, so the first one becomes ::.

sections.h: Every interface has several addresses, and each has a scope
sections.html:
Look at app's card in the lab network and count its IPv6 addresses. There are two, and after the next section there will be three. In IPv4 a card normally has one address. In IPv6 several at once is the design, and each address has a scope: how far away it means anything.

The first bits tell you which kind an address is:

Prefix Kind IPv4 relative
fe80::/10 link-local: valid on one link only 169.254.0.0/16
fc00::/7, in practice fd00::/8 unique local (ULA): private, never routed on the internet the RFC 1918 blocks
2000::/3 global unicast: public, routed everywhere public addresses
::1 loopback, this host 127.0.0.1
ff00::/8 multicast: one packet to every member of a group broadcast, roughly

There is no broadcast in IPv6. Multicast groups take over its jobs: ff02::1 is every node on the link and ff02::2 every router. Two prefixes you will see in examples: 2001:db8::/32 is reserved for documentation (RFC 3849), and a real ULA prefix has 40 random bits after fd (RFC 4193), so that two companies that merge don't collide the way two 10.0.0.0/8 networks do. The lab's fd00:10:6::/64 skips the random part to be easy to type.

A link-local address exists on every IPv6 card, and the host makes it itself before anyone configures anything. Here is how app got fe80::10fc:1ff:fe3b:eb52 from its MAC 12:fc:01:3b:eb:52. Take the six MAC bytes, flip the U/L bit from lesson 2 in the first byte (12 becomes 10), and put ff:fe in the middle. That gives the 64-bit interface ID 10fc:01ff:fe3b:eb52, and fe80:: goes in front. This recipe is modified EUI-64 (RFC 4291), and the Linux kernel uses it by default. It has a privacy problem: the same interface ID follows a laptop from network to network. So macOS, Windows and phones use random interface IDs that stay stable on one network (the idea of RFC 7217) and add temporary addresses that change daily for outgoing connections (RFC 8981).

Link-local addresses come with one surprise. Every link uses the same fe80::/64, so a host with two cards has no way to know which one you mean. You must name the card, the zone, after a %: fe80::e8cd:e9ff:fe43:37ae%eth0. Leave it out and ping warns and gets no answer. The JVM keeps the zone as the scope ID of an Inet6Address. Neighbor discovery and router advertisements, the next section, talk entirely in link-local addresses, which is why they work before any other address exists.

try.title: Derive a link-local address and ping it
steps: Print app's MAC and IPv6 routes, and api's link-local address. Work out app's link-local address from its MAC by hand (flip the 0x02 bit of the first byte, insert ff:fe) and compare it with what ip -6 addr showed in the last Try it.
Copy api's fe80:: address into LL and ping it twice: without a zone, then with %eth0. Predict which one works.

code.title: in labs/
code.html: docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app ip -br link show eth0 docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app ip -6 route docker compose -f env/net.yml exec api ip -6 addr show eth0 scope link LL=fe80::e8cd:e9ff:fe43:37ae # use api's address from the line above docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app ping -c 1 $LL docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app ping -c 1 $LL%eth0

MAC 12:fc:01:3b:eb:52 becomes 10fc:01ff:fe3b:eb52, so fe80::10fc:1ff:fe3b:eb52. The same works for api: its MAC ea:cd:e9:43:37:ae gives e8cd:e9ff:fe43:37ae. Without %eth0 the kernel doesn't know which link the address belongs to, and ping even tells you so. Note the routes: fe80::/64 is on every IPv6 card, and Docker's gateway fd00:10:6::1 is the default router.

sections.h: A host gives itself an address, and finds its neighbors without ARP
sections.html:
In IPv4 a host gets its address from a DHCP server, which hands out leases and keeps a table of who has which address, or from a person typing it in. IPv6 can use DHCPv6 too, but its usual way needs no server and no table: SLAAC, stateless address autoconfiguration (RFC 4862). The host builds its own address from a prefix that the router announces.

Build it up from the pieces you have. The host already has a link-local address. Before using it, the host checks that nobody else on the link has the same one. That check is duplicate address detection: a Neighbor Solicitation, "who has this address?", sent from the unspecified address :: because the host has no address of its own yet. If anyone answers, the address is taken. Then the host needs a prefix that is routed, and only a router knows one. So the router multicasts a Router Advertisement to ff02::1, every few minutes and whenever a host asks with a Router Solicitation. It says: this /64 is on this link, you may build your own address in it, and I can be your default router for 1,800 seconds. The host glues its interface ID behind the prefix, checks the new address the same way, and adds a default route via the router's link-local address. The router never learns which address the host took.

The same Neighbor Solicitation message replaces ARP, from lesson 2. Neighbor discovery (RFC 4861) is ICMPv6 inside IPv6, not a protocol of its own with its own EtherType. And the question doesn't go to every card on the link. It goes to the target's solicited-node multicast group: ff02::1:ff followed by the last 24 bits of the address you are looking for. For fd00:10:6::20 that is ff02::1:ff00:20. On Ethernet the frame goes to 33:33 plus the last 32 bits, 33:33:ff:00:00:20. That is a group MAC (the low bit of 33 is 1), and a card only takes it if it joined the group, so in practice only the owner's card looks at it. The answer, a Neighbor Advertisement, goes straight back by unicast, and the result sits in a neighbor table with ARP's states: REACHABLE, STALE, PROBE.

Step through it, then do it. Docker hands out IPv6 addresses itself and sends no router advertisements, so in the Try it api plays the router with a short Python script. That is also the weak spot of SLAAC: any host on the link can send an RA, and every host believes it. A misconfigured laptop can announce itself as everyone's default router. Office and data-centre switches filter RAs from ports that shouldn't send them, a feature called RA Guard (RFC 6105).

frames.say: api answers straight to app's MAC, and app caches it in the neighbor table with the same states as ARP's: REACHABLE, then STALE. Two messages, and no broadcast anywhere in this whole sequence.

One advertisement, and app built 2001:db8:6:0:10fc:1ff:fe3b:eb52 from the prefix plus its own interface ID, checked it from :: (up to a second later, a random delay the RFC asks for), and added a default route via api's link-local address (proto ra). The last line is api checking an address of its own: the bridge sent api its own advertisement back, and api believed it. Any host that hears an RA takes it seriously.

sections.h: Dual stack: one name, two addresses, and a race to connect
sections.html:
Many networks now run both protocols side by side, which is called dual stack. A name such as api then has an A record for its IPv4 address and an AAAA record for its IPv6 address, and a client that asks for both gets two answers. Which one should it connect to?

The simplest client tries the first address and, if that fails, the next. The operating system sorts the list so that IPv6 usually comes first (RFC 6724). That works until the IPv6 path is broken: a firewall drops it, or a home router has a half-working tunnel. Then every connection waits for the IPv6 attempt to time out before it tries IPv4. With Linux's default settings, a TCP connect gives up after about two minutes.

Happy Eyeballs (RFC 8305) races the two instead. Start the IPv6 connection. If it hasn't connected within a short delay, 250 ms recommended, start an IPv4 attempt as well, use whichever connects first and close the other. The user pays at most the delay, not the timeout. curl gives IPv6 a 200 ms head start, and Chrome and Firefox 300 ms.

The JVM does none of this, and it has its own ordering. InetAddress.getAllByName returns IPv4 addresses first by default (java.net.preferIPv6Addresses=false), the opposite of the operating system. Set the property to true and IPv6 comes first, or to system to keep the operating system's order. Either way, new InetSocketAddress(host, port) keeps only the first address, and Socket.connect and the JDK's HttpClient try only that one. In the Try it, with api's IPv6 port blocked, curl connects over IPv4 after 0.2 s, while a JVM that prefers IPv6 times out after its full 3-second connect timeout. With the default setting the JVM never uses IPv6 at all, even when it works.

A few more things change for your code once IPv6 traffic arrives:

  • Addresses don't fit in VARCHAR(15). The longest text form is 45 characters (ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:255.255.255.255), or store the 16 bytes as binary.
  • Put brackets around an IPv6 literal in a URL or a host:port setting: http://[fd00:10:6::20]:8080/. Code that splits host:port on a colon breaks.
  • A server bound to :: accepts IPv4 clients too, and many runtimes show them as IPv4-mapped addresses: ::ffff:10.10.6.10. Python's web server in the Try it logs exactly that. The JVM turns them back into Inet4Address, but your logs, load balancers and partners may not.
  • Rate-limit and block by /64, not by single address: one IPv6 host may legally use any of the 2^64 addresses in its subnet.
  • No NAT means a host's address can be reached from outside unless a firewall says otherwise. Lesson 3 warned that NAT is no firewall; in IPv6 the firewall has to be real.

try.title: Race IPv6 against IPv4, and watch the JVM not race
steps: Resolve api the way the C library does, then fetch from api over IPv4 and over IPv6 and read api's log. Predict how the IPv4 client appears in the log of a server bound to ::.

Run Dial.java on app. It prints the addresses in the JVM's order and connects the way most JVM code does, to the first address only. The lab box image has JDK 25, and one Java file runs without Gradle (labs/net/src/demo/java/sfz/net/l05/demo/Dial.java).

Break IPv6 on api with a firewall rule that drops its port 8080. Predict, then run: how long does curl take now, and what does the JVM do with and without -Djava.net.preferIPv6Addresses=true? Delete the rule at the end. When you are done with the lesson, docker compose -f env/net.yml down stops everything.

code.title: in labs/
code.html: docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app getent ahosts api docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app curl -s -4 http://api:8080/ docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app curl -s -6 http://api:8080/ docker compose -f env/net.yml logs --no-log-prefix api | tail -2 docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app java /labs/net/src/demo/java/sfz/net/l05/demo/Dial.java api 8080 docker compose -f env/net.yml exec api ip6tables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 8080 -j DROP docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app curl -sv -o /dev/null -w 'connected after %{time_connect} s\n' http://api:8080/ 2>&1 | grep -E 'Trying|Connected|connected after' docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app java /labs/net/src/demo/java/sfz/net/l05/demo/Dial.java api 8080 docker compose -f env/net.yml exec app java -Djava.net.preferIPv6Addresses=true /labs/net/src/demo/java/sfz/net/l05/demo/Dial.java api 8080 docker compose -f env/net.yml exec api ip6tables -D INPUT -p tcp --dport 8080 -j DROP

The C library lists IPv6 first and the JVM lists IPv4 first, for the same name. The server bound to :: logs the IPv4 client as ::ffff:10.10.6.10. The JVM prints its IPv6 address in the long form, without ::. With IPv6 blocked, curl tried IPv6, started IPv4 after 200 ms and connected over IPv4: Happy Eyeballs. The default JVM didn't notice anything, because it never tried IPv6. The JVM that prefers IPv6 waited out its whole 3-second timeout on one address and failed, although IPv4 worked.

analogy: An IPv6 address is like a postal address where the city prints the street name on a flyer and you choose your own house number. The router's advertisement is the flyer: "this street is 2001:db8:6". Each house picks a number, shouts it once down the street to check that no neighbour already uses it, and starts receiving mail. Nobody at the town hall writes down who lives where. The link-local address is the name you use for the person next door, which means nothing one street over, so you always say which street you mean (the %eth0). The analogy breaks on trust: a real street would notice a stranger handing out fake flyers, but on an IPv6 link any host can send a router advertisement and every other host will follow it.
world: Many mobile networks give phones IPv6 addresses, so requests from your card-payment app can reach your API gateway over IPv6 while your test traffic from the office uses IPv4. The gateway passes the client address on in X-Forwarded-For, and a Quarkus filter checks it against a partner allowlist, a fraud rule keyed by client address and a rate limiter. Each of those breaks in its own way: the allowlist compares strings and misses the long form the JVM prints, the Oracle column for the address is VARCHAR2(15), and the rate limiter counts per address while one phone can rotate through the 2^64 addresses of its /64. Parse addresses into InetAddress before comparing them, store them as RAW(16) or as canonical text up to 45 characters, and key rate limits on the /64. Inside your own network, check what your JVMs do on dual-stack Kubernetes: by default they connect over IPv4 only, and with -Djava.net.preferIPv6Addresses=true one broken IPv6 route turns every call into a connect timeout, because neither Socket nor HttpClient falls back to the next address.
mistake: The common mistake is treating an IP address as a string. With IPv4 it mostly works, because almost every tool prints 10.10.6.10 the same way. With IPv6 the same address has many legal spellings: the JVM prints fd00:10:6:0:0:0:0:20, nginx and Linux print fd00:10:6::20, and a dual-stack socket in many runtimes turns an IPv4 client into ::ffff:10.10.6.10. Allowlists then miss, rate limiters count one client twice, and log searches find half the requests. Parse every address into InetAddress (or 16 bytes) at the edge of your system, compare those, and when you must print or store text, use the RFC 5952 form from this lesson's lab.

compare.title: Finding a neighbor's MAC: ARP in IPv4, neighbor discovery in IPv6

a.label: IPv4: ARP
a.title: lesson 2, client asks for peer
a.html:
b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42:
    Request who-has 10.10.1.20 tell 10.10.1.10, length 28
3a:42:9a:52:90:f5 > b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42:
    Reply 10.10.1.20 is-at 3a:42:9a:52:90:f5, length 28

b.label: IPv6: neighbor discovery
b.title: this lesson, app asks for api
b.html:
12:fc:01:3b:eb:52 > 33:33:ff:00:00:20, ethertype IPv6 (0x86dd), length 86:
    fd00:10:6::10 > ff02::1:ff00:20: ICMP6, neighbor solicitation, who has fd00:10:6::20, length 32
ea:cd:e9:43:37:ae > 12:fc:01:3b:eb:52, ethertype IPv6 (0x86dd), length 86:
    fd00:10:6::20 > fd00:10:6::10: ICMP6, neighbor advertisement, tgt is fd00:10:6::20, length 32

compare.note: The question and answer are the same, and so is the unicast reply. What differs is where the question goes and what carries it. ARP is its own protocol straight on Ethernet (EtherType 0x0806) and asks every card on the link through the broadcast MAC. Neighbor discovery is ICMPv6 inside an ordinary IPv6 packet, so it has real IPv6 addresses, and it asks only the multicast group made from the target's last 24 bits. Every other card drops the frame in hardware without waking the kernel.

worked.title: From a MAC to a canonical IPv6 address, by hand

steps.say: app's card has MAC 12:fc:01:3b:eb:52. Modified EUI-64 turns 48 bits into a 64-bit interface ID. First flip the U/L bit, 0x02 of the first byte, the bit you read in lesson 2.
Then put ff:fe between the third and the fourth byte, and read the eight bytes as four 16-bit groups.
Put the link-local prefix fe80::/64 in front, which is fe80 followed by three zero groups, and write all eight groups in full.
Now RFC 5952. Drop the leading zeros in every group, then replace the longest run of two or more zero groups with ::. Here there is only one run, three groups long.
steps.code:
fe80:0:0:0:10fc:1ff:fe3b:eb52     no leading zeros
fe80::10fc:1ff:fe3b:eb52          the run of three zeros becomes ::

steps.say: Two cases catch people. When two runs are equally long, the first one gets ::. A single zero group never does. The lab's tests check both.

lab.title: An IPv6 address parser and formatter
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder. All 14 fail. An Ipv6 is eight 16-bit groups; toBytes, exploded and fromBytes are finished.
Write parse. Split the text on :: (at most two halves), parse each half's groups, and fill the gap with zero groups until there are eight. A dotted IPv4 tail counts as two groups.

Write format, RFC 5952: find the longest run of two or more zero groups (a later run must be strictly longer to win), print the groups before and after it in lower-case hex, and join them with ::. Handle IPv4-mapped addresses first.
Write kind from the prefixes on Ipv6Kind, then fromMac (modified EUI-64) and solicitedNode.

One test parses a real Neighbor Solicitation captured on app and checks that its destination is the solicited-node address of its target. Another feeds format what InetAddress.getHostAddress() returns. Run the tests until all 14 pass.
hints: "fd00:10:6".split(':') gives three groups; an empty half (as in ::1) gives none. Without :: you need exactly eight groups.
Int.toString(16) already drops leading zeros and prints lower case.
For format, walk the groups once, tracking the start and length of the current zero run and the best run so far. If the best run is shorter than 2, join all eight groups.
Link-local is groups[0] and 0xffc0 == 0xfe80; unique local is groups[0] and 0xfe00 == 0xfc00.

drill.title: Squeeze and classify
drill.prompt: No tools. Write each address in RFC 5952 form and name its kind (link-local, unique local, global, loopback, IPv4-mapped, multicast). Then answer: which MAC produced the first one? (a) FE80:0000:0000:0000:0202:B3FF:FE1E:8329 (b) 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329 (c) 0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1 (d) fd12:3456:789a:0001:0000:0000:0000:0000 (e) 2001:db8:0:0:1:0:0:1 (f) 0:0:0:0:0:ffff:c0a8:0101 (g) ff02:0:0:0:0:1:ff00:20

answer.html:
(a) fe80::202:b3ff:fe1e:8329        link-local
(b) 2001:db8::ff00:42:8329          global (documentation prefix)
(c) ::1                             loopback
(d) fd12:3456:789a:1::              unique local
(e) 2001:db8::1:0:0:1               global (tie: the first run gets ::)
(f) ::ffff:192.168.1.1              IPv4-mapped (c0a8 = 192.168, 0101 = 1.1)
(g) ff02::1:ff00:20                 multicast: the solicited-node group for ...:20

MAC behind (a): interface ID 0202:b3ff:fe1e:8329
  remove ff:fe        -> 02 02 b3 | 1e 83 29
  flip the U/L bit    -> 02 xor 02 = 00
  MAC 00:02:b3:1e:83:29 (a vendor-assigned card)

recap: An IPv6 address is 128 bits in eight hex groups. Leading zeros may go and one run of zero groups may become ::. RFC 5952 picks one form: lower case, the longest run, the first on a tie, never for a single group.
A card has several addresses at once: a link-local fe80:: one it makes itself, and unique local (fd00::/8) or global ones. Link-local addresses need a zone, such as %eth0.
SLAAC: a router advertises a /64, and each host appends its own 64-bit interface ID and checks the address with duplicate address detection. The router keeps no list.
Neighbor discovery replaces ARP with ICMPv6 sent to the target's solicited-node multicast group (ff02::1:ff plus its last 24 bits), so there is no broadcast at all.
Happy Eyeballs gives IPv6 a 250 ms head start and then races IPv4. The JVM doesn't race: it puts IPv4 first by default and connects to the first address only.

explain.prompt: A colleague asks how a laptop on a fresh IPv6 network gets an address when there is no DHCP server. Explain it step by step, and say what replaces ARP afterwards.
explain.answer: As soon as the card comes up, the laptop makes a link-local address by itself: fe80:: plus a 64-bit interface ID, either built from the MAC (flip one bit, insert ff:fe) or random. Before using it, it sends a neighbor solicitation from :: asking whether anyone already has that address, and if nobody answers it keeps it. Then it asks the routers on the link with a router solicitation, and a router answers with a router advertisement: here is the /64 prefix for this link, you may build your own address in it, and you can use me as your default router. The laptop puts its interface ID behind that prefix, checks the new address the same way, and adds a default route via the router's link-local address. The router keeps no record of it. To reach a neighbor later, the laptop sends a neighbor solicitation to the target's solicited-node multicast group, made from the last 24 bits of the target's address, and the owner answers with a unicast neighbor advertisement. That replaces ARP, and there's no broadcast anywhere.

deeper.html:
The IPv6 header. It is a fixed 40 bytes: version, a traffic class, a 20-bit flow label, payload length, next header (the IPv4 protocol field under a new name, 58 for ICMPv6), hop limit (the TTL under a new name), and the two addresses. There is no header checksum, because the link and the transport already check, so routers don't have to recompute one at every hop. Options moved into extension headers that sit between the IPv6 header and the payload, chained by their next-header fields.

No fragmentation in routers. An IPv6 router never splits a packet. It drops it and sends ICMPv6 Packet Too Big (type 2), the twin of lesson 4's Fragmentation Needed, and only the sender may fragment. Every IPv6 link must carry at least 1,280 bytes (RFC 8200), so a sender that stays at or below that never needs path MTU discovery. Blocking ICMPv6 type 2 breaks IPv6 even more reliably than blocking ICMP 3/4 breaks IPv4.

DHCPv6 and the flags. An advertisement carries two flags that SLAAC ignores in this lesson's script: M (managed) tells hosts to get addresses from DHCPv6, and O (other) tells them to get only other settings, such as DNS servers, from it. DNS servers can also ride in the advertisement itself (RFC 8106). Android doesn't implement DHCPv6 address assignment, so networks that phones must join keep SLAAC on.

IPv6-only networks. Many mobile networks give phones only an IPv6 address. To reach IPv4-only servers, the provider runs NAT64: a DNS64 resolver invents AAAA records inside 64:ff9b::/96 that embed the IPv4 address, and a gateway translates. That is one reason an IPv6 client can reach your IPv4-only API, and why your logs may show an address you never configured.
